set1.io: Discuss publication bias
set1.q: Why should publication bias always be considered when reading a review?
opts: Missing studies can distort the evidence
Correct, because a review can only include what has been published, so unpublished null results leave it looking at a skewed set of studies.
It affects only narrative reviews
It threatens any review that relies on published studies, including systematic reviews and meta-analyses, which is why it must always be considered.
A random effects model corrects it
Choosing a statistical model does not restore studies that were never published, so the model cannot correct this.
Two reviewers selecting studies removes it
Independent reviewers make selection consistent, yet they cannot include studies that were never published.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

set1.io: Discuss grading recommendations for treatment
set1.q: To which kinds of questions is grading of evidence most often applied?
opts: Prevalence and incidence
These describe how common disease is; grading recommendations targets decisions about what to do, such as treatment and screening.
Etiology and disease naming
Grading concerns recommended actions, and is most often used for treatment and screening rather than for these topics.
Anatomy and staging
Grades summarize evidence for action and apply mainly to treatment and screening.
Treatment and screening
Correct, and grading is a quick way to assess clinical significance, although it still involves some value judgment in weighing pros and cons.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

set1.io: Discuss grading recommendations for treatment
set1.q: What does a grade of 2A imply for the best action?
opts: It is the same for every patient
Uniform action for all patients is the implication of a strong recommendation, not a weak one.
It may vary with values
Correct, because the best action may differ with circumstances or values: a weak recommendation with high-quality evidence reflects benefits closely balanced with risks and burdens.
It rests on low-quality evidence
The letter A means the evidence is high quality, with consistent well-performed randomized controlled trials.
It should never be considered
A weak recommendation still identifies a reasonable option; it says only that the best action varies with the patient and the setting.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

set1.io: Discuss conflict of interest
set1.q: What happens after peer reviewers recommend acceptance?
opts: It is published with no further review
An editorial review of language and grammar still takes place between acceptance and publication.
The authors repeat the study
Repeating the study is not part of the process; acceptance is followed by editorial review and then publication.
Editors review language and grammar
Correct, and only then is the article published; peer review as a whole helps to counter conflict of interest.
Peer reviewers correct the grammar
Language and grammar are checked by editors after acceptance rather than by the peer reviewers.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 34

set1.io: Discuss grading recommendations for treatment
set1.q: When does the grading scheme give a weak recommendation?
opts: Benefits are closely balanced with risks
Correct, and uncertainty in the estimates of benefits, risks and burdens can also lead to a weak grade.
Risks clearly outweigh benefits
This yields a strong recommendation (against the treatment), since a strong grade covers benefits clearly outweighing risks 'or vice versa'.
Benefits clearly outweigh burdens
Clear benefit over risks and burdens gives a strong recommendation, graded 1.
Every study reports the same effect
Agreement among studies bears on evidence quality rather than on how closely benefits balance risks.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

set1.io: Discuss conflict of interest
set1.q: Which standard requires disclosure of members' financial, intellectual, institutional and patient or public interests?
opts: Transparency
Transparency means that how the guideline was developed and funded is explicit and publicly accessible.
External review
External review means the full spectrum of relevant stakeholders has reviewed the guideline.
Conflict of interest
Correct, because group members' conflicts related to financial, intellectual, institutional and patient or public activities bearing on the guideline are disclosed.
Updating
Updating means the guideline reports its publication date and evidence review and plans revision when new evidence arises.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 36

set1.io: Identify resources for answering clinical questions
set1.q: Which question is asked when reading beyond the abstract?
opts: How strong were the methods?
Correct, and the reader also asks how big the effect was, what limitations and biases existed, and what the author recommends.
What is the study about?
This is answered by quick reading of the abstract, which begins with what the study is about.
What was concluded?
The conclusion is read in the abstract, and reading beyond it tests whether that conclusion is supported.
Who does it apply to?
Whom the study applies to is asked during the quick reading of the abstract.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 39

set1.io: Discuss conflict of interest
set1.q: Why should conflicts of interest be acknowledged?
opts: So the study is excluded automatically
Disclosure does not exclude a study; it informs readers, who then judge whether bias is likely.
So readers can judge whether bias is present
Correct, because bias may be unintended or otherwise, and disclosure lets readers weigh how much to trust the results.
So that the findings become significant
Statistical significance depends on the data, and disclosure has no effect on the results.
So peer review becomes unnecessary
Peer review helps in addition to disclosure, and neither replaces the other.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 33

set1.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of systemic reviews
set1.q: A clinician wants one summary of a large body of studies to guide a decision. Which is helpful?
opts: A narrative review
A narrative review can be influenced by its author's values and may cite selectively, so it is a weaker basis for a decision.
A systematic review
Correct, because a systematic review summarizes bodies of evidence so clinicians can make decisions; good ones provide the highest level of evidence.
A single case report
A case report describes one patient and sits low in the hierarchy, so it cannot summarize a body of studies.
An expert's personal opinion
Opinion is at the base of the evidence hierarchy; a systematic review draws on the evidence in a structured, explicit way.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 29

set1.io: Discuss publication bias
set1.q: A systematic review searches only published articles. Which studies is it most likely to be missing?
opts: Studies with significant results
The opposite is true: results reaching significance are more likely to appear in print, which is what distorts the published record.
Studies with rigorous methods
Rigor does not decide publication in this way; the bias arises because results that fail to reach significance are less likely to be published.
Studies with very large samples
Size does not determine publication bias; a large study with a null result is still less likely to appear than one with a positive finding.
Studies without significant results
Correct, and it happens through editor preference and sponsors who are less willing to support research unfavorable to their product.
set1.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 46

set1.io: Identify resources for answering clinical questions
set1.q: Which question belongs to quick reading of an abstract?
opts: How big was the effect?
Size of effect is one of the questions asked when reading beyond the abstract.
What limitations existed and were they addressed?
Limitations and how they were handled are examined beyond the abstract.
Are the conclusions valid?
Correct, along with what the study is about, who it applies to, and whether it can and should be applied to your patients.
What impact will the results have?
Judging the impact of the results is part of reading beyond the abstract.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 38

set1.io: Identify resources for answering clinical questions
set1.q: The title and keywords of an article match the topic sought. What comes next when screening?
opts: Read the entire article
The whole article is read only after the abstract, summary and conclusion prove useful and relevant.
Read the abstract and conclusion
Correct, and the reader checks for clear aims, a well-defined hypothesis and precise conclusions before deciding whether to read on.
Skip to the next article
Skipping is the response to a title and keywords that do not match, and not to a match.
Check the reference list first
The flow of screening goes from title and keywords to the abstract, summary and conclusion, not to the references.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 40

set1.io: Identify methods to conduct a systematic review
set1.q: Which two statistical tests are named for assessing heterogeneity?
opts: Cochran's Q and the I-squared statistic
Correct, and both quantify how much study results differ, which guides whether and how the results can be pooled.
Kaplan-Meier and log-rank tests
These are used to analyze time to an event, not to measure how much results differ among studies.
Pearson and Spearman correlation
Correlation coefficients measure association between two variables, not differences among the results of several studies.
Mann-Whitney and Wilcoxon tests
These compare groups of measurements; heterogeneity between studies is assessed with Cochran's Q and the I-squared statistic.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

set1.io: Discuss grading recommendations for treatment
set1.q: Which grade is a strong recommendation supported by high-quality evidence?
opts: 1A
Correct: the benefits clearly outweigh risks and burdens, and the evidence is consistent, from well-performed randomized controlled trials.
1C
A grade of 1C is also a strong recommendation, but its evidence is low quality, coming from observational studies or flawed trials.
2A
A grade of 2A has high-quality evidence, but it is a weak recommendation, because benefits are closely balanced with risks and burdens.
2C
A grade of 2C is a weak recommendation with low-quality evidence, described as very weak.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

set1.io: Discuss grading recommendations for treatment
set1.q: What is the purpose of grading evidence?
opts: A replacement for clinical judgment
Guidelines should be used with the best clinical judgment, and a grade cannot substitute for it.
A quick way to assess clinical significance
Correct, though some value judgment remains, because the pros and cons still have to be weighed.
A guarantee that a treatment works
A grade expresses confidence in an estimate and the strength of a recommendation, and cannot guarantee an outcome.
A measure of statistical significance alone
Grading expresses clinical significance and weighs benefits against risks, which goes beyond a statistical test.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 30

set1.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of narrative reviews
set1.q: Which strength is typical of a narrative review?
opts: It answers one predetermined clinical question
That describes a systematic review, whose goal is a specific, predetermined question; a narrative review is valued for its breadth.
It applies explicit rules for choosing studies
Explicit selection rules belong to a systematic review, whereas a narrative review is unstructured and its author picks what to cite.
It produces a pooled numerical estimate of effect
Pooling numerical results is what a meta-analysis does; a narrative review summarizes the evidence in words as an expert sees it.
It can cover broad topics and many issues
Correct, because an expert summary is not tied to a single question, so it can range across a whole disease and the issues around it.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 4

set1.io: Identify resources for answering clinical questions
set1.q: Which of these is a suggested way to keep current?
opts: Sales representatives
Sales representatives have a commercial interest, and are not among the suggested sources, which are organizations, journals, colleagues and patients.
Advertising
Advertising is promotion rather than appraised evidence, and the suggested sources are organizations, journals, colleagues and patients.
Patients
Correct, and the others suggested are professional organizations, journal articles and colleagues.
Press releases
Press releases summarize results without appraisal; suggested sources are professional organizations, journals, colleagues and patients.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 37

set1.io: Identify methods to conduct a systematic review
set1.q: What should a systematic review list for each excluded study?
opts: The reason it was excluded
Correct, because listing excluded studies together with the rationale lets a reader judge whether the criteria were applied fairly.
The reviewer's personal opinion of it
Personal opinion is not the requirement; explicit criteria based on the study question and design should justify each exclusion.
The date each study was rejected
The timing of a decision does not let readers judge the selection; the rationale for exclusion does.
The name of the reviewer who disagreed
Naming dissenters is not called for; a list of excluded studies with the rationale is.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

set1.io: Identify methods to conduct a systematic review
set1.q: How is the pooled summary shown on a forest plot?
opts: As a diamond
Correct, because the diamond marks the summary effect from pooling, shown as the summary of the pooled studies.
As a pyramid
A pyramid is the way the hierarchy of evidence is drawn, not the way a pooled result is displayed.
As a funnel
A funnel plot is a different figure, used to check for publication and reporting bias.
As a circle
The pooled summary on a forest plot is drawn as a diamond rather than as a circle.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

set1.io: Identify methods to conduct a systematic review
set1.q: How are the studies in a systematic review summarized?
opts: Scatter plots and life tables
These display other kinds of data; the summary step uses forest plots and tables of the studies' characteristics.
Nomograms and receiver operating characteristic curves
Those are tools for interpreting diagnostic tests, and the summary step uses forest plots and tables of characteristics.
Funnel plots and dose-response curves
A funnel plot assesses publication bias and is used at the selection step; summarizing relies on forest plots and characteristic tables.
Forest plots and tables of characteristics
Correct, because figures such as forest plots show results across studies, and tables set out the characteristics of each one.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

set1.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of narrative reviews
set1.q: Which topic suits a narrative review better than a systematic review?
opts: Whether one drug lowers mortality more than another
A focused comparison of two treatments on one outcome is the kind of specific, predetermined question a systematic review is built to answer.
Whether a new test detects a disease more accurately
A question about the accuracy of one test is specific and answerable, which is the setting for a systematic review of test studies.
Whether screening lowers deaths in one age group
This names a population, an intervention and an outcome, so it is a focused question that a systematic review can answer.
An overview of many aspects of a disease
Correct, because narrative reviews suit broad topics and a range of issues, whereas a systematic review needs a focused question.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 4

set1.io: Discuss conflict of interest
set1.q: Which is a way conflict of interest can manifest?
opts: Random assignment of participants
Random assignment protects against bias in a trial, and is not a way that a conflict of interest shows itself.
Calculation of confidence intervals
Confidence intervals are a statistical tool for precision, not a manifestation of conflicting interests.
Blinding of outcome assessors
Blinding limits bias; it is a safeguard rather than a sign of conflict of interest.
Selective reporting of results
Correct, and other manifestations are the choice of studies in reviews and meta-analyses, and exaggeration or fabrication of results.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 33

set1.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of meta-analysis
set1.q: A meta-analysis combines one high-quality trial with several seriously flawed studies. Which appraisal question does this raise?
opts: Was a forest plot drawn for the review?
Whether a figure exists does not address the mismatch in quality among the pooled studies.
Are the studies all of equal quality?
Correct, because the quality of the included studies should be examined, and mixing very different levels of quality weakens the pooled result.
Did the reviewers write a protocol first?
A protocol concerns how the review was planned, whereas the concern here is the level of the studies combined.
Were the excluded studies all listed?
Listing excluded studies shows how selection was done; the problem in this scenario is the mix of quality among included ones.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

set1.io: Identify the components of a PICO question: Patients, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes
set1.q: Which question contains all four components of a well-built clinical question?
opts: In adults with migraine, does daily propranolol reduce the number of headache days?
This has patients, an intervention and an outcome, but no comparison, so the reader does not know the alternative it was measured against.
Does daily propranolol, compared with placebo, work better than other treatments?
This has an intervention and a comparison, but it defines no patient group and no measurable outcome, so it cannot be answered from studies.
In adults with migraine, does daily propranolol, compared with placebo, reduce headache days?
Correct, because it names the patients (adults with migraine), intervention (propranolol), comparison (placebo) and outcome (headache days).
In adults with migraine, is propranolol better, compared with placebo, in some way?
This has patients, an intervention and a comparison, but 'better in some way' names no specific outcome to be measured.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 8

set1.io: Identify methods to conduct a systematic review
set1.q: Which methods explore reasons for differences among studies?
opts: Subgroup analysis, sensitivity analysis and metaregression
Correct, and subgroups can be based on study quality and other factors; the text should also discuss the role of bias and study factors.
Blinding, randomization and allocation concealment
These are ways of protecting a single trial from bias, and they do not explore differences among pooled studies.
Fixed weighting, rounding and narrative summary
Weighting is part of pooling, and none of these is a recognized way to explore why study results differ.
Forest plots, nomograms and receiver operating characteristic curves
Figures summarize or interpret results; exploring the reasons for differences requires subgroup, sensitivity or metaregression analysis.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

set1.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of narrative reviews
set1.q: Why are authors of narrative reviews often well placed to write them?
opts: They follow a written protocol set in advance
A prospective protocol identifies the question and analysis of a systematic review; narrative reviews are unstructured and usually have none.
They are free of financial or personal influence
Authors of narrative reviews may be influenced by their own values and experience, so freedom from influence cannot be assumed.
They usually treat patients with the disease
Correct, because authors of narrative reviews usually have experience caring for patients with the disease, which lends the summary clinical perspective.
They have read every published study on the topic
Nothing guarantees completeness: cited articles may be selected to support a point of view rather than to cover all the evidence.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 4

set1.io: Identify methods to conduct a systematic review
set1.q: A reviewer leaves out a trial with only a handful of participants. Which question about sampling the best studies guided this?
opts: Was the research peer-reviewed?
Peer review is a separate check on quality, and this trial was left out because of its size rather than its review status.
Was the sample size sufficient?
Correct, because a study too small to give a reliable estimate is weighed against the others when the best studies are sampled.
Is the information still current?
Currency asks whether more recent studies exist; it does not address the number of participants.
What were the limitations?
Limitations is a broader appraisal question, whereas a handful of participants points specifically to insufficient sample size.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 19

set1.io: Discuss conflict of interest
set1.q: A trade group's guideline endorses only products sold by its member companies. Which conflict of interest is this?
opts: Financial conflict of interest
Financial conflict concerns funding and personal gain for authors or their families rather than benefit to an organization.
Institutional conflict
Correct, because institutional conflict arises when a recommendation benefits one organization more than others.
Personal conflict of interest
Personal conflicts involve an author's own biases and career, not the interests of a sponsoring organization.
Intellectual conflict of interest
Intellectual conflict sits with personal biases and career interests of authors, not with benefit to one organization.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 32

set1.io: Discuss publication bias
set1.q: How does publication bias differ from reporting bias?
opts: Reporting bias concerns whole studies not being published
This reverses them: reporting bias means a study appears but only a subset of its data is made available.
Both concern errors in how participants were assigned
Assignment errors are selection problems within a study; these two biases concern what reaches the literature.
Publication bias concerns whole studies not being published
Correct, because non-significant research is less likely to be published, whereas reporting bias concerns only a subset of a study's data being made available.
Both are removed by a larger sample size
A bigger sample reduces chance but does nothing about results that are never published or partly reported.
set1.cite: 1 PAJ5512 Introduction Bias Validity MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 45

set1.io: Discuss grading recommendations for treatment
set1.q: What do the letters A, B and C in a recommendation grade indicate?
opts: The strength of the recommendation
Strength is shown by the numbers 1 and 2, where 1 is strong and 2 is weak.
The size of the patient group
Population size is not part of the grade; the letters reflect the quality of the evidence.
The cost of the treatment
Cost does not feature in the grade, which combines strength of recommendation with quality of evidence.
The quality of the supporting evidence
Correct: the letters express confidence in the estimate of effect, with A the highest, based on the type and quality of studies behind it.
set1.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

set2.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of narrative reviews
set2.q: Why may the validity of a narrative review be questionable?
opts: It is unstructured
Correct, because with no set method for finding, choosing or appraising studies, a reader cannot judge how reliable the conclusions are.
It states its search method in detail
Reporting how studies were found is a strength that a systematic review provides, and it would raise rather than lower confidence.
It weights each study by its size
Weighting studies belongs to a meta-analysis; a narrative review does not pool results, so weighting cannot explain doubts about its validity.
It lists every excluded study and the reason
Listing excluded studies with the rationale is a safeguard of systematic reviews, and a narrative review typically does not do so.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: Discuss the principles of meta-analysis
set2.q: Two trials enroll 250 and 750 participants. If a meta-analysis weights each in proportion to size, what share of the weight goes to the smaller trial?
opts: Fifty percent would be equal weighting; weighting in proportion to size gives the smaller trial 250 out of 1,000, which is 25 percent.
Thirty-three percent comes from the ratio 250 to 750 rather than the share of the total; the share is 250 out of 1,000, or 25 percent.
Seventy-five percent is the share of the larger trial (750 out of 1,000); the smaller trial carries 25 percent.
Correct: 250 of the 1,000 total participants is 25 percent, so the larger trial contributes three times as much weight as the smaller one.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 22

set2.io: Discuss grading recommendations for treatment
set2.q: How should clinicians treat a strong recommendation such as 1A?
opts: Follow it only when a patient specifically requests it
A strong recommendation applies to most patients whether or not they request it; patient values matter more for weak recommendations.
Follow it unless a compelling rationale supports an alternative
Correct, because strong recommendations apply to most patients in most circumstances without reservation.
Choose whichever approach best matches each patient's values
Tailoring to circumstances or patient and societal values is the implication of a weak recommendation, such as 2A.
Apply it to a minority of patients under some circumstances
That is the reverse: a strong recommendation applies to most patients, and alternatives are better for some patients only under weak grades.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

set2.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of systemic reviews
set2.q: Which findings are summarized for the studies located in a systematic review?
opts: Journal, year and reputation of the authors
Publication details may be tabulated, but the summary of results turns on effect size, precision and validity rather than on prestige.
Funding source and cost of each study
Funding matters for conflict of interest, yet the summary of the results concerns effect size, precision and validity of the studies.
Length and language of each report
These are characteristics of the reports; what a summary must convey is how large the effects were, how precise, and how valid.
Effect size, precision and validity
Correct, and validity is judged both internally (for the sample studied) and externally (for other settings), alongside how many quality studies were found.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 20

set2.io: Discuss conflict of interest
set2.q: A researcher's promotion depends on publishing a positive result. Which conflict of interest is this?
opts: Financial conflict of interest
Financial conflicts concern who funded the research and who benefits financially, not advancement of a career.
Institutional conflict of interest
Institutional conflicts arise when a recommendation benefits one organization more than others.
Personal or career conflict
Correct: personal, intellectual or career conflicts include personal biases and professional benefits the author stands to gain.
Regulatory conflict of interest
This is not a category named for conflicts of interest; the categories are financial, personal, intellectual, career and institutional.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 32

set2.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of systemic reviews
set2.q: A reader asks how the studies in a systematic review were located. Which question belongs with it?
opts: Which reviewer wrote the discussion section?
Who drafted a section says nothing about the quality of the review; appraisal concerns the search, the criteria, and the original studies.
Which inclusion and exclusion criteria were used?
Correct, because how studies were found and which criteria decided their entry are read together with how valid the original studies were.
How many pages does the reference list run?
Length of the reference list is not an appraisal criterion; the question is whether the criteria for including studies were explicit.
Were the tables printed in color?
Presentation style does not bear on validity; the reader needs to know how studies were found, selected and judged.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 27

set2.io: Discuss grading recommendations for treatment
set2.q: What evidence supports a 1C recommendation?
opts: Observational studies, unsystematic experience or flawed trials
Correct, and any estimate of effect from such evidence is uncertain, although benefits still appear to outweigh risks and burdens.
Consistent evidence from well-performed randomized trials
That describes 1A, in which further research is unlikely to change confidence in the estimates of benefits and risks.
Randomized trials with important limitations
That describes 1B; the evidence behind 1C is of lower quality still.
Overwhelming evidence from several trial designs
Overwhelming evidence in some other form belongs to the highest quality of evidence, graded A.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

set2.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of narrative reviews
set2.q: Which element may a narrative review leave out?
opts: An expert summary of the evidence
The expert summary is the defining feature of a narrative review, so it is always present rather than left out.
A critique of the original research
Correct, because narrative reviews may not critique the studies they cite, so a reader cannot tell whether the evidence behind a claim is strong.
Recommendations for clinical practice
Narrative reviews usually give recommendations along with the summary, so this is provided rather than missing.
A view across a broad range of issues
Breadth is one of the advantages of a narrative review, so a wide range of issues is normally covered.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: Discuss publication bias
set2.q: Which tool is named for assessing publication and reporting bias in a review?
opts: Nomograms
A nomogram converts pretest probability and a likelihood ratio into posttest probability, which is a diagnostic-test tool.
Receiver operating characteristic curves
These plot true positive rate against false positive rate to compare tests, and do not assess publication bias.
Life tables
Life tables describe survival over time and have no role in checking whether studies are missing.
Funnel plots
Correct, and the assessment is done while selecting studies, alongside the explicit criteria and the listing of excluded studies.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

set2.io: Discuss conflict of interest
set2.q: What do good guidelines give along with their recommendations?
opts: The authors' personal preferences
Personal preference is not evidence; good guidelines show the evidence and reasoning behind each recommendation.
The supporting evidence and rationale
Correct, and clinicians should still apply their own best clinical judgment when deciding whether to use a guideline in practice.
A ruling that judgment is not needed
Guidelines support rather than replace clinical judgment, which should always be applied when using them.
Only the results of the largest trial
A guideline draws on systematic reviews of the evidence and not merely on the largest trial.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 35

set2.io: Discuss the principles of meta-analysis
set2.q: How does a meta-analysis combine numerical results?
opts: By averaging them equally whatever the size
Equal averaging would let a tiny study count as much as a large one; the analysis gives more weight to larger, more precise studies.
By selecting the single largest study
Pooling uses all the similar studies, and using only the largest would discard information rather than combine it.
By giving larger, more precise studies more weight
Correct, and the result is a more precise estimate of the effect than any single study gives; study size is the main driver of that precision.
By counting how many studies were positive
Counting positive studies ignores effect size and precision; a meta-analysis combines the numerical results with weights.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 22

set2.io: Discuss conflict of interest
set2.q: A guideline gives the reasoning, the level of confidence in the evidence, and the strength of each recommendation. Which standard is met?
opts: Evidence and strength
Correct, because each recommendation is accompanied by its underlying reasoning, the confidence in the evidence, and its strength.
Description of recommendations
That standard means the guideline states precisely what the recommended action is and under what circumstances it should be performed.
Systematic review
That standard means recommendations are based on systematic reviews that met high standards for quality.
Group composition
That standard concerns a multidisciplinary, balanced membership rather than how each recommendation is supported.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 36

set2.io: Discuss conflict of interest
set2.q: A guideline panel includes methodologic experts, clinicians and members of the affected population. Which standard is met?
opts: External review
External review concerns stakeholders assessing the finished guideline, whereas this describes who sat on the panel that wrote it.
Group composition
Correct, because the panel is multidisciplinary and balanced, with a variety of methodologic experts, clinicians and populations affected by the guideline.
Transparency
Transparency concerns making the development and funding of the guideline explicit and publicly accessible.
Updating
Updating concerns publication dates and plans to revise the guideline when new evidence would change it.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 36

set2.io: Identify the components of a PICO question: Patients, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes
set2.q: A clinical question asks whether a new inhaled steroid, compared with the current one, reduces exacerbations in everyone. Which element most needs to be refined?
opts: The comparison
The comparison is already stated as the current inhaled steroid, so it is defined; the weakness lies with the group described.
The outcome
Exacerbations are a specific, measurable outcome, so this element is already defined.
The intervention
The new inhaled steroid is a clearly named intervention, so it needs no refinement.
The population
Correct, because 'everyone' is too broad; a more specific population, such as a defined age group or severity, should be stated for the question to be useful.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 18

set2.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of meta-analysis
set2.q: Under which circumstance may a meta-analysis be misleading?
opts: The included studies all measure the same outcome
Studies with a common outcome are what pooling requires, so similarity in this respect makes combining more appropriate.
The included studies are not similar
Correct, and the strength of the value judgment about whether studies are similar enough to combine should be considered.
The pooled sample is larger than any single study
A larger pooled sample gives a more precise estimate, which is an advantage of the method.
The inclusion criteria were written down in advance
Explicit criteria are very important to a meta-analysis and make the results less likely to mislead.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

set2.io: Discuss publication bias
set2.q: A meta-analysis pools only journal articles, and trials showing no benefit of a drug were never published. What is the likely effect?
opts: The pooled benefit may be overstated
Correct, because the missing trials are the ones showing little or no effect, so the published set makes the drug look better than it is.
The pooled benefit will be understated
Unpublished trials here are the ones with no benefit, so removing them pushes the pooled estimate toward benefit and not away from it.
The pooled estimate will be unaffected
Excluding a systematically different group of studies changes the estimate; that is why publication bias must always be considered.
Heterogeneity will disappear
Leaving out unpublished studies does not remove real differences among those included, and the estimate remains biased.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 28

set2.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of meta-analysis
set2.q: Which is an advantage of a meta-analysis?
opts: A stronger, more precise estimate of effect size
Correct, because combining similar studies narrows the uncertainty around the effect compared with any one of them alone.
Immunity to flaws in the included studies
The opposite applies: a meta-analysis is only as good as the studies included, so their flaws carry into the pooled result.
No need for inclusion and exclusion criteria
The criteria are very important, because they decide which studies are pooled.
Freedom from publication bias
Publication bias should always be considered, since a pooled analysis can include only the studies that were made available.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 25

set2.io: Discuss grading recommendations for treatment
set2.q: Why is a 1B recommendation graded below a 1A?
opts: Its trials have important limitations
Correct, because 1B rests on randomized trials with inconsistent results, methodologic flaws or imprecision, so further research may change confidence.
Its benefits do not clearly outweigh risks
Both 1A and 1B are strong recommendations, in which benefits clearly outweigh risks and burdens.
It rests only on observational studies
Observational studies, unsystematic experience or seriously flawed trials describe 1C, which is graded lower than 1B.
It is a weak recommendation
Both are strong recommendations, and the difference lies in the quality of the evidence behind them.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 31

set2.io: Identify the components of a PICO question: Patients, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes
set2.q: What may the intervention element name besides a treatment?
opts: An outcome to be measured
The outcome is a separate element, describing what one hopes to accomplish, measure, improve or affect.
The alternative to be compared
The alternative is the comparison element, a separate part of the question distinct from the intervention.
A prognostic factor or an exposure
Correct, because the second element covers whatever main intervention, prognostic factor or exposure is under consideration, so it suits risk and prognosis questions.
A description of similar patients
Describing a group of similar patients is the job of the patient, population or problem element.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: Identify the components of a PICO question: Patients, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes
set2.q: For a question comparing two diagnostic tests, which outcome fits?
opts: Number of tests ordered
Test volume describes practice patterns rather than how accurately a test detects the disease of interest.
Sensitivity and specificity
Correct, because a question about how well a test detects disease can name the accuracy of each test, expressed as sensitivity and specificity, as its outcome.
Patient satisfaction with the result
Satisfaction is a patient-reported result and does not measure whether a test correctly separates those with and without the disease.
Length of the clinic visit
Visit length is a process measure and does not show whether either test identifies disease more accurately.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 14

set2.io: Discuss the principles of meta-analysis
set2.q: What does the fixed effect model assume?
opts: Effect sizes that vary for reasons beyond chance
Allowing variation not due to chance is the assumption of the random effects model, used when heterogeneity is present.
An effect that differs in every study
If every study had its own effect, pooling to one fixed magnitude would not be justified; the fixed effect model assumes one magnitude.
No effect at all in any study
The model assumes a fixed magnitude for the effect size, which need not be zero.
One fixed effect size, with variation due to chance
Correct, and it is used when there is no significant heterogeneity, which means the studies appear similar enough to share one effect.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 23

set2.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of meta-analysis
set2.q: What is a fundamental limitation of a meta-analysis?
opts: It cannot combine numerical results
Combining numerical results is exactly what it does, weighting them in proportion to study size.
It always reduces the total sample size
Pooling enlarges the sample, since it adds the participants of the studies together; sample size is not reduced.
It can address only rare complications
It can examine benefits, harms, complications and subgroups, and is not restricted to rare complications.
It is only as good as the included studies
Correct, because combining poor studies produces a larger, more confident poor estimate, so the quality of the pooled studies must be checked.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 26

set2.io: Identify the components of a PICO question: Patients, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes
set2.q: A clinical question asks whether physical therapy, compared with daily naproxen, reduces pain in adults with knee osteoarthritis. Which element is the comparison?
opts: Physical therapy
Physical therapy is the intervention, the main treatment being considered, rather than the alternative it is compared with.
Adults with knee osteoarthritis
That describes the patients or population, the group of patients similar to the ones the question is about.
Daily naproxen
Correct, because the comparison is the main alternative set against the intervention, here the anti-inflammatory drug that physical therapy is measured against.
Reduction in pain
Pain reduction is the outcome, what the investigators hope to measure or improve, and is not the alternative treatment.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: Identify methods to conduct a systematic review
set2.q: Who should confirm that the selection of studies was consistent?
opts: At least two reviewers
Correct, because independent agreement between reviewers checks that the criteria were applied consistently; the same is done when assessing each study's risk of bias.
One experienced reviewer
A single reviewer cannot show that the criteria were applied consistently, since there is no second judgment to compare with.
The lead author alone
One person deciding alone leaves selection unchecked; consistency is confirmed by at least two reviewers.
The journal editor
Editors handle the manuscript after it is submitted; confirming consistent study selection is part of how the reviewers conduct the review.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 21

set2.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of narrative reviews
set2.q: A review of a treatment cites only trials that favor the author's preferred therapy. Which limitation does this show?
opts: Heterogeneity was not tested statistically
Testing heterogeneity applies when results are pooled in a meta-analysis; the problem here is the author's selective choice of articles.
The pooled estimate was weighted by study size
A narrative review does not pool data at all; selective citation is the concern, because it can make one point of view look like the consensus.
The review was limited to a single narrow question
A narrow question is a feature of a systematic review; a narrative review usually covers broad topics, which leaves room for selective citing.
Cited articles may be chosen to prove a point
Correct, because with no structured method for finding studies, an author can pick the articles that support a view and leave out the rest.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: Identify resources for answering clinical questions
set2.q: In a cursory review, where does the reader look to learn to whom a study applies?
opts: The title
The title tells what the study is about, not whom it applies to.
Patients and setting
Correct, because in the cursory review the question 'to whom does it apply?' is answered from the description of the patients and setting.
The design
The design shows whether the findings are likely to be true rather than to whom they apply.
The conclusions
The conclusions state what was found to be the case, and do not describe to whom the study applies.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 41

set2.io: Identify the components of a PICO question: Patients, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes
set2.q: A clinical question asks whether nebulized hypertonic saline, compared with normal saline, shortens hospital stay in infants with bronchiolitis. Which element is the outcome?
opts: Infants with bronchiolitis
That is the patient or population element: the group of patients the answer is meant to apply to, not the result being measured.
Nebulized hypertonic saline
That is the intervention, the main treatment under consideration, rather than the result the investigators want to measure.
Length of hospital stay
Correct, because the outcome is what one hopes to accomplish, measure, improve or affect, here how long the infants remain in the hospital.
Normal saline
Normal saline is the comparison, the alternative against which the intervention is judged, rather than the outcome.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: Identify the components of a PICO question: Patients, Intervention, Comparison, Outcomes
set2.q: A clinical question asks whether heavy alcohol use, compared with none, is linked to esophageal cancer among middle-aged smokers. Which element is the exposure?
opts: Esophageal cancer
Esophageal cancer is the outcome, the event one hopes to measure, not the exposure that may lead to it.
Middle-aged smokers
That names the patients or population, the group described so the answer can be applied to similar people.
Heavy alcohol use
Correct, because the intervention element can be an exposure or prognostic factor rather than a treatment, and here it is the factor whose effect is asked about.
No alcohol use
Abstaining from alcohol is the comparison, the alternative to the exposure, rather than the exposure itself.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: Identify resources for answering clinical questions
set2.q: In an in-depth review, where does the reader look to see how big the effect was?
opts: The introduction
The introduction shows the importance of the research question, not the size of the effect.
The methods
The methods answer how strong the research methods were rather than how big the effect was.
Figures and tables
Correct, because the size of the effect is read from the figures and tables, while methods show how strong the study was.
The discussion
The discussion gives context for the results, and the size of the effect itself is read from figures and tables.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 41

set2.io: Discuss the advantages and limitations of systemic reviews
set2.q: Which consideration helps decide whether a review question can be answered?
opts: Whether strong studies exist and agree
Correct, because the availability of strong studies, how many there are, and whether they agree all shape whether a focused question can be answered.
Whether the authors already favor an answer
An author's preference is a source of bias rather than a consideration; the question should be judged by the evidence that exists.
Whether every study was published in one journal
The evidence base is judged by strength, number and agreement of studies, not by whether they share a publisher.
Whether an expert has written on the topic before
Prior expert commentary does not show that answerable studies exist; the number and strength of the studies matter.
set2.cite: 10 PAJ5512 Clinical Questions and Reviews MBF_2026sc.pptx, Slide 7
